docs.title: Welcome to DIB Documentation.
docs.text:
A prototype distributed Edge-to-Cloud system for automating industrial technical inspections (RaaS - Robot as a Service).

This project simulates a ground infrastructure (Hangar) and a flight unit (Drone) communicating in real time through a central MQTT broker, ensuring a secure, fault-tolerant architecture based on Finite State Machines (FSM).

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: The following is an index with all the chapters: 1. Analysis 2. Architecture 3. Protocol 4. Behaviour 5. Design 1. Control 2. Hangar 3. Drone 4. Backend and dashboard 5. Simulators 6. Hardware 7. Testing 8. Deployment 9. Conclusions

docs.title: 1. Project goal
docs.text:
The goal of the project is to build a working prototype of a Drone-in-a-Box (DIB) system: an autonomous drone that lives in a ground station (the hangar), leaves it to perform automated industrial inspections (e.g. thermographic monitoring of a photovoltaic plant) and comes back to recharge, without a human pilot.

The prototype focuses on the coordination and safety logic between the drone and the hangar, rather than on real flight:

  • the hangar is a physical device that controls its door, monitors the local environment and decides autonomously whether a take-off or a landing is safe;
  • the drone is a physical board that simulates a flight and streams realistic telemetry;
  • a central backend supervises the whole system, shows its live state on a dashboard and lets an operator issue commands. The three subsystems are independent and communicate only through messages, following a publish/subscribe architecture.

The board is physically moved in and out of the hangar during take-off and landing Drone battery – charge and discharge model Drone attitude (tilt) tilt sensor, if available in the kit roll/pitch angles otherwise Communication Wi-Fi + MQTT between real devices –

docs.title: 2. Requirements
docs.text: Requirements are numbered so that they can be traced to the design and to the tests.

docs.title: 2.1 Functional requirements
docs.text:
Hangar

ID Requirement FR-H1 The hangar shall open and close its door on its own decision, moving it gradually. FR-H2 The hangar shall periodically sample temperature and humidity. FR-H3 The hangar shall classify the environment as safe or unsafe according to configurable thresholds, and report the reason when unsafe. FR-H4 The hangar shall evaluate every take-off request and grant it only if the environment is safe and the presence sensor detects the drone inside. FR-H5 The hangar shall authenticate the drone before evaluating a landing request. FR-H6 The hangar shall evaluate every landing request and grant it only if the drone is authenticated, the environment is safe and the drone is stable (tilt and speed within limits). FR-H7 The hangar shall notify a grant only when the door is fully open, and close the door once the drone has left or landed. FR-H8 Every denial shall carry a machine-readable reason. FR-H9 The hangar shall show its current state through LEDs and display. FR-H10 The hangar shall publish its state, door position and environmental data. FR-H11 The hangar shall allow resetting the alarm locally, through a button, when the backend is not available. FR-H12 The hangar shall detect whether the drone is physically inside, through a presence sensor.

Drone

ID Requirement FR-D1 While at rest in the hangar, the drone shall recharge its (simulated) battery. FR-D2 The drone shall request permission before taking off and before landing, and act only after a grant. FR-D3 The drone shall simulate a mission as a sequence of segments, and report its progress. FR-D4 The drone shall simulate and publish telemetry: battery level, speed, acceleration, altitude, ground distance, distance from the hangar, tilt and error state. FR-D5 The drone shall return to the hangar when the mission is complete, when the battery falls below a return threshold, or when recalled by the operator. FR-D6 If a landing is denied, the drone shall hold its position and retry periodically. FR-D7 The drone shall enter an emergency state on critical anomalies (excessive tilt, critical battery, internal fault). FR-D8 The drone shall answer the hangar's authentication challenge.

Backend and dashboard

ID Requirement FR-B1 The backend shall collect the state and data published by the hangar and the drone. FR-B2 The dashboard shall show, in real time, the hangar state, door state and environmental data (with recent history). FR-B3 The dashboard shall show, in real time, the drone state, battery, kinematics, distance from the hangar, tilt, mission progress and errors. FR-B4 The dashboard shall show whether each device is online or offline. FR-B5 The dashboard shall keep a log of state transitions, requests and decisions. FR-B6 The operator shall be able to start a mission, recall the drone, trigger an emergency door closure and reset an alarm. FR-B7 Operator commands are requests: the devices may refuse them, and every refusal shall be reported with a reason.

docs.title: 2.2 Non-functional requirements
docs.text: ID Category Requirement NFR-1 Safety Safety-critical decisions (opening the door, granting take-off or landing) shall be taken locally by the hangar and shall not depend on the backend being available. NFR-2 Safety When communication with the drone is lost during an operation, the hangar shall move to a safe state. NFR-3 Reliability Every request shall be answered or time out; no device shall wait forever. NFR-4 Reliability Devices shall reconnect automatically after a Wi-Fi or broker outage and keep working autonomously while disconnected. NFR-5 Reliability The disconnection of a device shall be detected by the others and by the backend. NFR-6 Responsiveness The hangar shall react to a request within 500 ms (excluding the door movement). NFR-7 Responsiveness The dashboard shall show telemetry with a delay of at most 2 s. NFR-8 Security Every client shall authenticate to the message broker; anonymous access shall be disabled. NFR-9 Security Each client shall be allowed to publish and subscribe only to the topics required by its role. NFR-10 Security The drone authentication shall resist replay of previously captured messages. NFR-11 Maintainability The control logic shall be independent of the hardware, so that it can be tested on a PC. NFR-12 Testability Each device shall be replaceable by a software simulator implementing the same protocol. NFR-13 Extensibility The message format and topic structure shall allow adding more drones or hangars in the future.

docs.title: 2.3 Constraints
docs.text:
• Hardware: 2 × Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W, 9 g servo motor, environmental sensors, LEDs and display (Keyestudio-style kit).
  • Communication: MQTT over Wi-Fi (TCP/IP).
  • Firmware language: C++.
  • Backend: runs on a PC (broker, supervision logic, dashboard).

docs.title: 3.1 Glossary
docs.text: Term Meaning Hangar Ground station that hosts, protects and recharges the drone. Door Movable cover of the hangar, driven by a servo motor. Environment reading One sample of temperature, humidity and water/steam presence. Safety policy Set of thresholds that classifies the environment as safe or unsafe. Mission A flight made of consecutive segments; its progress is the travelled fraction of the total length. Request A take-off or landing request sent by the drone; identified by a reqId. Decision The hangar's answer to a request: granted or denied, with a reason. Challenge Random value (nonce) sent by the hangar that the drone must sign to prove its identity. Holding The drone hovering near the hangar while waiting for a landing grant. Supervision unit Backend component that observes the system and forwards operator commands. Operator Human user of the dashboard.

docs.title: 4.1 Actors
docs.text:
• Operator: monitors the system and issues commands from the dashboard.
  • Drone: autonomous actor that requests take-off and landing.
  • Hangar: autonomous actor that decides on requests and controls the door.
  • Environment: external source of weather conditions (time, temperature, humidity, rain).

docs.title: 4.2 Use case overview
docs.text: ID Use case Primary actor UC-1 Monitor the system Operator UC-2 Start a mission Operator UC-3 Take off Drone UC-4 Execute a mission Drone UC-5 Return and land Drone UC-6 Recall the drone Operator UC-7 Emergency door closure Operator UC-8 Reset an alarm Operator

docs.title: 4.3 Main scenarios
docs.text:
UC-1 Monitor the system

  1. The operator opens the dashboard.
  2. The dashboard shows the latest known state of hangar and drone, even if they published it before the dashboard was opened.
  3. The dashboard updates state, environment and telemetry as new data arrives, and logs every transition and decision.
  4. If a device goes offline, the dashboard marks it as offline. UC-2 Start a mission

Precondition: the drone is at rest inside the hangar.

  1. The operator presses Start mission.
  2. The supervision unit forwards the command to the drone.
  3. The drone checks that its battery is above the minimum take-off level.
  4. The drone starts UC-3. Alternative 3a: the battery is too low → the drone refuses the command with reason BATTERY_LOW; the dashboard shows the refusal.

UC-3 Take off

Precondition: the drone is at rest inside the hangar, the door is closed.

  1. The drone sends a take-off request.
  2. The hangar evaluates the environment: it is safe.
  3. The hangar opens the door.
  4. When the door is fully open, the hangar grants the take-off.
  5. The drone leaves the hangar and climbs to cruise altitude.
  6. The drone notifies that it has left; the hangar closes the door.
  7. The drone is in mission (UC-4). Alternative 2a: the environment is unsafe → the hangar denies the request with the reason (e.g. HUMIDITY_HIGH, WATER_DETECTED); the door stays closed; the drone stays at rest.

Alternative 1a: the hangar does not answer within the timeout → the drone gives up and stays at rest, reporting NO_RESPONSE.

UC-4 Execute a mission

  1. The drone flies the mission segments, accelerating and decelerating on each one.
  2. The drone publishes telemetry and mission progress periodically.
  3. When the last segment is completed, the drone starts UC-5. Alternative 1a: the battery falls below the return threshold → the drone interrupts the mission and starts UC-5. Alternative 1b: a critical anomaly occurs (excessive tilt, fault) → the drone enters the emergency state and reports it.

UC-5 Return and land

  1. The drone flies back towards the hangar.
  2. When it is close enough, the drone sends a landing request.
  3. The hangar sends an authentication challenge.
  4. The drone answers the challenge; the hangar verifies it.
  5. The hangar checks environment and drone stability: both are fine.
  6. The hangar opens the door; when it is fully open, it grants the landing.
  7. The drone descends and notifies that it has landed.
  8. The hangar closes the door; the drone is at rest and starts recharging. Alternative 4a: authentication fails → the hangar denies the landing with reason AUTH_FAILED; the door stays closed. Alternative 5a: environment unsafe or drone unstable → the hangar denies the landing with the reason; the drone holds its position and retries periodically (back to step 2).

UC-6 Recall the drone

Precondition: the drone is in mission.

  1. The operator presses Recall.
  2. The drone interrupts the mission and starts UC-5. Alternative 2a: the drone is not in mission → the command is refused with reason INVALID_STATE.

UC-7 Emergency door closure

  1. The operator presses Emergency close.
  2. The hangar closes the door and enters the alarm state; it denies new requests until reset. Alternative 2a: the drone is passing through the door (taking off or landing) → see edge case EC-15.

UC-8 Reset an alarm

  1. The operator presses Reset alarm.
  2. If the cause of the alarm is no longer present, the hangar leaves the alarm state; otherwise it refuses with the cause as reason.

docs.title: 5. Edge cases
docs.text:
Edge cases describe situations outside the main scenarios and the expected behaviour of the system. Each one becomes at least one test scenario.

ID Situation Expected behaviour EC-1 The environment becomes unsafe while the door is open for a take-off, before the drone has left. The take-off already granted is completed (aborting halfway is more dangerous); the hangar closes the door right after and denies new requests. EC-2 After a take-off grant, the drone never reports that it has left. After a timeout the hangar closes the door only if the drone is confirmed inside or offline, and raises an alarm. EC-3 The drone loses connection while landing (door open). The hangar detects the disconnection, waits for a grace period, then closes the door and raises an alarm. EC-4 The hangar loses connection while the drone is in mission. The drone completes its mission; landing requests time out, so the drone holds and retries until the hangar is back or the battery becomes critical (EC-6). EC-5 The backend is not available. Drone and hangar keep coordinating directly; only monitoring and operator commands are lost. EC-6 A device that is not the registered drone, or uses a wrong key, requests a landing. Authentication fails; the landing is denied with AUTH_FAILED; the door stays closed. EC-7 A previously captured authentication answer is sent again (replay). The answer does not match the new challenge; authentication fails. EC-8 A message is duplicated, or an answer arrives for an old request. Answers are matched by reqId; answers for unknown or expired requests are ignored. EC-9 An operator command is not valid in the current state (e.g. Start mission while in mission). The command is refused with INVALID_STATE; the state does not change. EC-10 The broker restarts, or the dashboard connects after the devices. The dashboard receives the last known state of each device as soon as it subscribes. EC-11 The hangar reboots while the drone is in mission. At start-up the hangar assumes the door must be closed and the drone outside unless the drone's last published state says otherwise. EC-12 An emergency closure is requested while the drone is passing through the door. The hangar completes the passage before closing (it does not close the door onto the drone), then enters the alarm state.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The system is composed of three main subsystems that communicate only through an MQTT broker:

  • Drone unit: a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W that simulates an autonomous inspection drone. It runs the flight state machine, requests permission to take off and land, and publishes its state and telemetry. A tilt sensor detects the inclination of the board, while the flight data (speed, acceleration, altitude, ground distance, distance from the hangar, mission progress) and the battery level are simulated.
  • Hangar unit: a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W that acts as the drone's ground station, sheltering it between missions. It opens and closes its door with a servo motor, monitors the environment (temperature, humidity and water/steam), and shows its state through LEDs and a display. It is the safety authority of the system: it authenticates the drone and grants or denies every take-off and landing request based on the local environmental conditions.
  • Backend: a set of services running on a PC.
    • The MQTT broker (Mosquitto) relays all messages between the components.
    • The control unit observes the whole system and forwards the operator's commands (start mission, recall, emergency closure, alarm reset) to the devices, which may refuse them.
    • The dashboard shows the real-time state of the drone and the hangar, and lets the operator issue commands.

Drone and hangar coordinate directly through the broker: the backend supervises the system but is not involved in safety-critical decisions, so the two devices keep working even if it is unavailable.

docs.title: Architectural style
docs.text:
The system follows a publish/subscribe architecture built around a central MQTT broker. Components never address each other directly: each one publishes messages on topics and subscribes to the topics it is interested in.

This style fits the system for three reasons:

  • Decoupling: drone and hangar do not need to know each other's network address, and a device can be replaced by a software simulator without changing the others.
  • Many-to-many communication: the same message reaches every interested component. The control unit and the dashboard observe all the traffic without the devices being aware of them.
  • Broker features: retained messages give a late subscriber the last known state of each device, and the Last Will mechanism notifies everyone when a device disconnects unexpectedly.

MQTT has no native request/response interaction, which the take-off and landing requests need. It is built on top of publish/subscribe with dedicated request and response topics, correlated by a request identifier and bounded by timeouts (see Protocol).

docs.title: Distribution of control
docs.text:
Safety-critical decisions are taken at the edge, by the hangar: opening the door, authenticating the drone, and granting or denying take-off and landing. The hangar evaluates every request against its own sensor readings, and it does not need the backend to do so.

The backend only supervises. Commands are requests, not orders: each device checks them against its current state and may refuse them with a reason.

As a consequence, drone and hangar keep coordinating directly through the broker even when the control unit or the dashboard are unavailable. Only monitoring and manual commands are lost. If the broker itself fails, no mission can start or end, but the hangar keeps the door closed and the drone holds its position until the connection is restored.

docs.title: Technology choices
docs.text: Option Decision Reason MQTT Adopted Publish/subscribe with a broker, QoS levels, retained messages and Last Will cover the needs of the system. It crosses firewalls, since every component acts as a client of the broker. CoAP Rejected It offers native request/response with confirmable messages, but no publish/subscribe and no broker: the control unit would have to know and poll each device. It would also lose retained state and Last Will. It is designed for low-power, lossy networks, which is not the case here. Thread / Matter Rejected Thread requires an IEEE 802.15.4 radio, which the Pico 2 W does not have (its radio supports only Wi-Fi and Bluetooth). Matter targets interoperability between smart-home products; its SDK is heavy and it adds nothing for a two-device industrial prototype. Wi-Fi Adopted Built into the Pico 2 W and supports TCP/IP directly. Its limits (range of about 150 m, high power consumption) are acceptable for a prototype; a real system would use a cellular or long-range radio link.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
MQTT provides little security by itself, so it is added at two levels.

Broker level

  • Anonymous access is disabled: every client authenticates to the broker with its own username and password.
  • Access control lists (ACLs) restrict each client to the topics required by its role, so a client cannot impersonate another one:
Client Can publish Can subscribe hangar dib/hangar/# dib/drone/#, dib/cmd/hangar drone dib/drone/# dib/hangar/#, dib/cmd/drone controlunit dib/cmd/# dib/#

Application level

Before evaluating a landing request, the hangar authenticates the drone with an HMAC-based challenge-response that resists replay attacks (see Protocol).

Known limitation: traffic is not encrypted (no TLS), so credentials travel in clear text on the local network. This is accepted for a prototype on an isolated network and listed among the future improvements.

docs.title: Behaviour
docs.text: This chapter models the behaviour of the system with finite state machines (FSMs). It defines the state machines of each device, how they interact with each other, and why they are designed as synchronous Moore machines.

docs.title: 1.1 Discrete and continuous components
docs.text: The system contains both kinds of components described in the theory: - discrete components evolve through atomic changes (a door is closed or opening, a request is granted or denied). They are modelled with FSMs; - continuous components evolve smoothly: the flight kinematics (speed, acceleration, altitude, distance) and the battery charge. They are not FSMs: they are modelled as simple equations, integrated with a fixed time step dt, e.g. v(t + dt) = v(t) + a · dt.

docs.title: 1.2 Extended FSMs
docs.text: All machines are extended FSMs (EFSMs): besides the discrete state, they use variables (timers, counters, the door angle, the current reqId). This keeps the number of discrete states small. Timeouts, for example, are counters of reactions, not additional states.

docs.title: 1.3 Globally asynchronous, locally synchronous
docs.text:
The two devices run on two different microcontrollers, with no shared clock. Their FSMs are therefore concurrent and asynchronous with respect to each other: they coordinate only by exchanging messages, and a message produced by one machine is an input event for the other (section 5).

On each device, instead, the machines are synchronous (time-triggered): they react periodically, with a fixed period. Time is part of the specification: timeouts, the gradual movement of the door, sensor sampling, the time step of the flight simulation. This scheme is known as GALS (globally asynchronous, locally synchronous).

Several synchronous FSMs run concurrently on the same device, one per task, each with its own period (section 6).

docs.title: 2.1 The choice
docs.text:
All FSMs in the system are designed as Moore machines. In the diagrams, the outputs are written inside each state, and the transitions are labelled only with their guards.

Outputs are of two kinds: - level outputs, held for the whole time the machine is in a state: the door command, the servo angle, the LED pattern, the active flight dynamics, the state published on MQTT; - messages, emitted once when the machine enters a state (entry actions, as in UML statecharts): a message is a discrete event, so sending it at every reaction while in the state would be wrong.

docs.title: 2.2 Why Moore and not Mealy
docs.text:
1. The published state is the output. Each device publishes its current state on a retained MQTT topic. With a Moore machine that state fully describes what the device is doing, so other components can rely on it. For example, the hangar does not need a separate "I have landed" message: it observes that the drone's state has become AT_REST. The protocol gets simpler, and the dashboard shows exactly what drives the outputs.
  2. Idempotent outputs after a failure. Since every output is bound to a state, it can be reproduced at any time from the state alone.
  3. Simpler implementation and tests. Each state is a class with an onEnter() method (messages) and an output function (levels), following the State pattern. A unit test checks a single fact: "after reaching state X, the outputs are Y". Trade-offs accepted. A Moore machine reacts to an input one reaction later than the equivalent Mealy machine, and sometime needs a few extra transient states (e.g. DENYING, section 4.1). With a period of 100 ms, the extra latency is at most 100 ms per step, well within the 500 ms of NFR-6.

Every state publishes its name on dib/drone/state when entered. The transitions to EMERGENCY drawn from IN_MISSION, RETURNING and HOLDING apply to every flying state (LEAVING, LANDING_REQ, AUTH_RESPONSE, LANDING included). They are omitted from the diagram for readability.

State Meaning AT_REST Inside the hangar, recharging. Initial state. TAKEOFF_REQ Take-off requested, waiting for the hangar's decision. LEAVING Leaving the hangar and climbing to cruise altitude. During this phase the board is taken out of the hangar. IN_MISSION Flying the mission segments. Reaching this state tells the hangar that the drone is out. RETURNING Flying back towards the hangar. LANDING_REQ Landing requested, hovering, waiting for the authentication challenge. AUTH_RESPONSE Challenge answered, waiting for the decision. HOLDING Landing denied or not answered: hovering until the retry timer expires. LANDING Descending into the hangar. During this phase the board is put back into the hangar. Reaching AT_REST tells the hangar that the drone has landed. EMERGENCY Critical anomaly: emergency descent in the safe area (EC-6). Left only by an operator reset after recovery. Variable Use reqId Identifier of the current request, used to match the answer. timer Counts reactions, for timeouts and for the retry delay. segment, progress Current mission segment and travelled fraction. battery, altitude, groundDistance, distanceFromHangar, tilt Read from the continuous models. fault Set by the anomaly input (section 3.2).

The guard startMission is true only if the command passed the dispatcher, which also checks that the battery is above the minimum take-off level. Otherwise it answers BATTERY_LOW.

The board is physically moved during take-off and landing, so the simulated LEAVING and LANDING phases last long enough to do it by hand (5–8 s each).

docs.title: 3.2 Anomaly input
docs.text: The tilt switch injects a fault to demonstrate the emergency behaviour: tilting the board makes the drone enter EMERGENCY. The switch is a digital input that bounces like a button, so it is read through the debouncing FSM of section 4.5, and its event sets the fault variable read by the flight FSM. Roll and pitch in the telemetry remain simulated, since the switch reports only tilted or not tilted.

docs.title: 3.3 Status LED
docs.text:
An RGB LED shows the drone state. Like the hangar indicator, its colour is a function of the flight FSM state.

Flight state Colour AT_REST green TAKEOFF_REQ, LANDING_REQ, AUTH_RESPONSE yellow blinking LEAVING, LANDING yellow IN_MISSION, RETURNING blue HOLDING blue blinking EMERGENCY red blinking

docs.title: 4. Hangar
docs.text: The hangar runs five FSMs: the controller, which takes decisions; the door, which executes them; the environment monitor, which conditions the temperature and humidity readings; the presence monitor, which detects whether the drone is inside; the button, which detects the local alarm reset. A sixth component, the status indicator, maps the controller state to the traffic light and the display.

docs.title: 4.1 Controller FSM
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
[*] --> IDLE

state "IDLE" as IDLE
IDLE : doorCmd = CLOSE
state "TAKEOFF_PREP" as TAKEOFF_PREP
TAKEOFF_PREP : doorCmd = OPEN
state "DEPARTURE" as DEPARTURE
DEPARTURE : doorCmd = OPEN
DEPARTURE : on entry send GRANTED
state "DRONE_OUT" as DRONE_OUT
DRONE_OUT : doorCmd = CLOSE
state "AUTHENTICATING" as AUTHENTICATING
AUTHENTICATING : doorCmd = CLOSE
AUTHENTICATING : on entry send CHALLENGE with nonce
state "LANDING_PREP" as LANDING_PREP
LANDING_PREP : doorCmd = OPEN
state "LANDING_WAIT" as LANDING_WAIT
LANDING_WAIT : doorCmd = OPEN
LANDING_WAIT : on entry send GRANTED
state "DENYING" as DENYING
DENYING : doorCmd = CLOSE
DENYING : on entry send DENIED with reason
state "ALARM" as ALARM
ALARM : doorCmd = CLOSE
ALARM : alarm = ON

IDLE --> TAKEOFF_PREP : TAKEOFF_REQ and envOk and droneDetected
IDLE --> DENYING : TAKEOFF_REQ and not envOk
IDLE --> DENYING : TAKEOFF_REQ and not droneDetected
TAKEOFF_PREP --> DEPARTURE : doorState = OPEN
DEPARTURE --> DRONE_OUT : droneState = IN_MISSION and not droneDetected
DRONE_OUT --> AUTHENTICATING : LANDING_REQ
AUTHENTICATING --> LANDING_PREP : hmac ok and envOk
AUTHENTICATING --> DENYING : hmac ok and not envOk
AUTHENTICATING --> DENYING : hmac wrong or timeout
LANDING_PREP --> LANDING_WAIT : doorState = OPEN
LANDING_WAIT --> IDLE : droneState = AT_REST and droneDetected
DENYING --> IDLE : droneDetected
DENYING --> DRONE_OUT : not droneDetected
IDLE --> ALARM : emergencyClose
DRONE_OUT --> ALARM : emergencyClose
DEPARTURE --> ALARM : timeout or droneOffline
LANDING_WAIT --> ALARM : timeout or droneOffline
ALARM --> IDLE : reset and causeCleared and droneDetected
ALARM --> DRONE_OUT : reset and causeCleared and not droneDetected

Every state publishes its name on dib/hangar/state when entered.

State Meaning IDLE Drone inside, door closed. TAKEOFF_PREP Take-off accepted, door opening. DEPARTURE Door fully open, take-off granted, waiting for the drone to be out. DRONE_OUT Drone in mission, door closed. AUTHENTICATING Landing requested, challenge sent, waiting for the answer. LANDING_PREP Landing accepted, door opening. LANDING_WAIT Door fully open, landing granted, waiting for the drone to land. DENYING Transient: sends the denial with its reason, then returns at the next reaction. ALARM Door closed, every request denied with ALARM_ACTIVE until a reset.

At start-up the controller enters IDLE; at its first reaction, if the presence monitor does not detect the drone, it moves to DRONE_OUT (EC-14).

Denial reasons set when entering DENYING:

Transition Reason take-off with not envOk BAD_WEATHER take-off with not droneDetected DRONE_NOT_PRESENT landing with hmac ok and not envOk BAD_WEATHER landing with hmac wrong AUTH_FAILED landing with timeout AUTH_TIMEOUT

Alarm causes set when entering ALARM:

Transition Cause emergencyClose EMERGENCY_CLOSE timeout in DEPARTURE DEPARTURE_TIMEOUT timeout in LANDING_WAIT LANDING_TIMEOUT droneOffline DRONE_OFFLINE

The guard causeCleared is always true for EMERGENCY_CLOSE, since a human decision is revoked by a human. For the other causes it is true when the drone is online again and its state agrees with the presence sensor.

Variable Use reqId, nonce Current request and authentication challenge. reason, cause Reason of the denial, cause of the alarm. timer Timeouts in AUTHENTICATING, DEPARTURE and LANDING_WAIT. emergencyPending Emergency closure requested while the drone is passing through the door (EC-15).

Inputs: envOk comes from the environment monitor (4.3), droneDetected from the presence monitor (4.4), doorState from the door FSM (4.2). droneState and droneOffline come from the drone's state topic and Last Will. reset comes from the dashboard or from the local button (4.5). Requests, the challenge answer and operator commands come from the dispatcher.

Two independent confirmations. Every passage through the door needs both the state declared by the drone and the physical detection by the presence sensor. If they do not agree before the timeout, the hangar enters the alarm state (EC-17).

docs.title: 4.2 Door FSM
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> CLOSED

  state "CLOSED" as CLOSED
  CLOSED : servo angle = 0°
  state "OPENING" as OPENING
  OPENING : servo angle = angle
  state "OPEN" as OPEN
  OPEN : servo angle = 90°
  state "CLOSING" as CLOSING
  CLOSING : servo angle = angle

  CLOSED --> OPENING : doorCmd = OPEN
  OPENING --> OPEN : angle >= 90°
  OPENING --> CLOSING : doorCmd = CLOSE
  OPEN --> CLOSING : doorCmd = CLOSE
  CLOSING --> CLOSED : angle <= 0°
  CLOSING --> OPENING : doorCmd = OPEN

In OPENING and CLOSING the variable angle increases or decreases by a fixed step at every reaction (e.g. 3° every 50 ms, a full movement in 1.5 s). The door state and its position in % are published at every change.

The door FSM is a pure executor: it never decides whether opening is safe. That decision belongs to the controller.

docs.title: 4.3 Environment monitor FSM
docs.text:
Raw readings are noisy, and a value near a threshold would make the classification flip at every sample. The monitor applies input conditioning: a change of classification requires several consecutive readings that agree.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> SAFE

  state "SAFE" as SAFE
  SAFE : envOk = true
  state "UNSAFE" as UNSAFE
  UNSAFE : envOk = false

  SAFE --> UNSAFE : unsafeCount >= 2
  UNSAFE --> SAFE : safeCount >= 3

unsafeCount and safeCount count consecutive readings that violate, or respect, the temperature and humidity thresholds of the safety policy, and are reset when a reading disagrees. A failed or invalid reading counts as unsafe (EC-12). Leaving the unsafe classification requires more readings than entering it, so the system is cautious.

docs.title: 4.4 Presence monitor FSM
docs.text:
An infrared sensor pointed at the parking spot detects whether the drone is inside. Its output can flicker (reflections, ambient light, the drone being moved), so a change is accepted only after several consecutive readings that agree.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> ABSENT

  state "ABSENT" as ABSENT
  ABSENT : droneDetected = false
  state "PRESENT" as PRESENT
  PRESENT : droneDetected = true

  ABSENT --> PRESENT : presentCount >= 3
  PRESENT --> ABSENT : absentCount >= 3

presentCount and absentCount count consecutive readings in which the sensor sees, or does not see, the drone. With a period of 100 ms, a change is confirmed in 300 ms. The initial state is corrected within the first reactions, so the controller knows where the drone is right after a reboot (EC-14). Every change is published together with the hangar state, so the dashboard can show it.

docs.title: 4.5 Button FSM (debouncing)
docs.text:
A local button on the hangar resets the alarm. It is the recovery channel when the backend is not reachable: without it, the hangar would stay in ALARM until the dashboard comes back. A press is accepted only while the controller is in ALARM, and only if the cause of the alarm has been cleared; otherwise the display shows CAUSE_NOT_CLEARED. Presses in any other state are ignored. The same machine reads the drone's tilt switch (3.2).

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> RELEASED

  state "RELEASED" as RELEASED
  RELEASED : no output
  state "PRESSED" as PRESSED
  PRESSED : on entry emit pressed event

  RELEASED --> PRESSED : pin = HIGH
  PRESSED --> RELEASED : pin = LOW

Debouncing follows from the choice of the period, as described in the theory:

  • the sampling period is 50 ms, longer than the typical bouncing period (~20 ms), so the bounces of a single press are not observed as separate presses;
  • the period is shorter than the minimum event separation time of a human press (a press lasts well over 100 ms), so no press is lost.

docs.title: 4.6 Status indicator
docs.text:
The status indicator is not an independent decision maker: its output is a function of the controller state. It is a Moore machine whose only internal state is the blinking phase, which toggles every 250 ms. It drives the traffic light and the 128×32 display.

Controller state Green Yellow Red Display IDLE on off off state, temperature, humidity TAKEOFF_PREP, LANDING_PREP off blinking off "DOOR OPENING" DEPARTURE, LANDING_WAIT off on off "TAKE-OFF" / "LANDING" DRONE_OUT blinking off off "DRONE OUT", temperature, humidity AUTHENTICATING off blinking off "AUTHENTICATING" DENYING off off on denial reason ALARM off off blinking alarm cause

docs.title: 5. Interaction between drone and hangar
docs.text: The two flight-critical interactions are request/response exchanges, matched by reqId and bounded by timeouts on both sides (NFR-3).

docs.title: 5.1 Take-off
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant D as Drone
  participant H as Hangar
  participant DR as Door

  Note over D: AT_REST
  D->>H: TAKEOFF_REQ (reqId)
  Note over D: TAKEOFF_REQ
  Note over H: IDLE, envOk, droneDetected
  H->>DR: doorCmd = OPEN
  Note over H: TAKEOFF_PREP
  DR-->>H: doorState = OPEN
  H->>D: GRANTED (reqId)
  Note over H: DEPARTURE
  Note over D: LEAVING, board taken out
  D-->>H: state = IN_MISSION
  Note over H: sensor no longer detects the drone
  H->>DR: doorCmd = CLOSE
  Note over H: DRONE_OUT

docs.title: 5.2 Landing with authentication
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant D as Drone
  participant H as Hangar
  participant DR as Door

  Note over D: RETURNING
  D->>H: LANDING_REQ (reqId)
  Note over D: LANDING_REQ
  H->>D: CHALLENGE (reqId, nonce)
  Note over H: AUTHENTICATING
  D->>H: AUTH_RESPONSE (reqId, HMAC(key, nonce, droneId, reqId))
  Note over D: AUTH_RESPONSE
  Note over H: hmac ok, envOk
  H->>DR: doorCmd = OPEN
  Note over H: LANDING_PREP
  DR-->>H: doorState = OPEN
  H->>D: GRANTED (reqId)
  Note over H: LANDING_WAIT
  Note over D: LANDING, board put back
  D-->>H: state = AT_REST
  Note over H: sensor detects the drone
  H->>DR: doorCmd = CLOSE

docs.title: 5.3 Landing denied
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant D as Drone
  participant H as Hangar

  D->>H: LANDING_REQ (reqId = 7)
  H->>D: CHALLENGE (7, nonce)
  D->>H: AUTH_RESPONSE (7, hmac)
  Note over H: hmac ok, not envOk
  H->>D: DENIED (7, BAD_WEATHER)

  Note over D: HOLDING, retry timer
  D->>H: LANDING_REQ (reqId = 8)

docs.title: 6. Tasks and periods
docs.text:
Each FSM is executed by one task of a cooperative scheduler. The continuous models are tasks too, since they advance with a fixed time step.

Device Task Executes Period Hangar Comm MQTT client, dispatcher, message queue 50 ms Hangar Controller Controller FSM (4.1) 100 ms Hangar Door Door FSM (4.2) 50 ms Hangar EnvMonitor Environment monitor FSM (4.3) 2 s Hangar Presence Presence monitor FSM (4.4) 100 ms Hangar Button Button FSM (4.5) 50 ms Hangar Status Status indicator (4.6) 250 ms Drone Comm MQTT client, dispatcher, message queue 50 ms Drone Flight Flight FSM (3.1) 100 ms Drone FlightModel Kinematics, dt = 100 ms 100 ms Drone Battery Battery model 1 s Drone Anomaly Button FSM on the tilt switch (3.2) 50 ms Drone StatusLed Status LED (3.3) 250 ms Drone Telemetry Publishes telemetry 500 ms

The choice of the periods follows the rule from the theory: the largest period that still guarantees that no event is lost and that latencies stay acceptable.

  • 100 ms for the decision-making FSMs gives a worst-case reaction latency well below the 500 ms of NFR-6.
  • 100 ms for the presence sensor confirms a change in 300 ms, far quicker than the time needed to move the drone in or out.
  • 50 ms for the door gives a smooth movement. For the button and the tilt switch it filters bounces while staying below the MEST of a press.
  • 2 s for the environment: the weather changes slowly, and the DHT11 sensor must not be read more than once per second.
  • The scheduler runs at 50 ms, the greatest common divisor of all periods.

Messages and the MEST. For physical inputs, choosing a period shorter than the MEST guarantees that no event is lost. Network messages give no such guarantee: two messages can arrive a few milliseconds apart. For this reason the MQTT callback never touches the FSMs: it pushes each message into a queue, and the dispatcher delivers the queued events to the machines at their next reaction. The queue is the boundary between the asynchronous world of the network and the synchronous world of the FSMs.

docs.title: Topic structure
docs.text: All topics start with dib/ and follow the pattern dib/<device>/<kind>. Topics are grouped below by publisher.

docs.title: Hangar topics
docs.text: Topic Subscriber QoS Retained dib/hangar/state control unit 1 yes dib/hangar/door control unit 0 yes dib/hangar/environment control unit 0 yes dib/hangar/response drone, control unit 1 no dib/hangar/cmd-reply control unit 1 no dib/hangar/status drone, control unit 1 yes

docs.title: Drone topics
docs.text: Topic Subscriber QoS Retained dib/drone/state hangar, control unit 1 yes dib/drone/telemetry control unit 0 no dib/drone/request hangar, control unit 1 no dib/drone/cmd-reply control unit 1 no dib/drone/status hangar, control unit 1 yes

docs.title: Control unit topics
docs.text: Topic Subscriber QoS Retained dib/cmd/drone drone 1 no dib/cmd/hangar hangar 1 no

docs.title: Topic descriptions
docs.text:
Topic Content state Current state of the device's main state machine. door Door state (CLOSED, OPENING, OPEN, CLOSING) and position in %. environment Temperature, humidity, water/steam detection and the safe/unsafe classification with its reason. telemetry Battery, speed, acceleration, altitude, ground distance, distance from the hangar, tilt, mission progress, error code. request Messages from the drone to the hangar: TAKEOFF_REQ, LANDING_REQ, AUTH_RESPONSE. response Messages from the hangar to the drone: CHALLENGE, GRANTED, DENIED. cmd Operator commands forwarded by the control unit. cmd-reply Result of a command: accepted, or refused with a reason. status online when the device connects; offline published by the broker as the device's Last Will.

The message type (e.g. TAKEOFF_REQ or LANDING_REQ) is a field of the JSON payload, not part of the topic name.

docs.title: Design rules
docs.text:
• Retained messages are used for topics that describe the current situation (state, door, environment, status), so that a component connecting late immediately receives the last known value.
  • Non-retained messages are used for events (requests, responses, commands, replies): delivering an old request to a component that has just connected would make it look like a new one. Telemetry is not retained either, because it changes continuously.
  • QoS 1 (at least once) is used where losing a message would block or confuse the system: states, requests, responses, commands. Duplicates are discarded thanks to the request identifier.
  • QoS 0 (at most once) is used for periodically sampled data: if a sample is lost, the next one arrives shortly after.

docs.title: Message format
docs.text:
All messages are JSON objects with the same envelope:

{
  "v": 1,
  "type": "TAKEOFF_REQ",
  "src": "drone",
  "ts": 128450,
  "reqId": 3482,
  "data": { }
}
Field Type Meaning v integer Protocol version, currently 1. type string Message type (see below). src string Sender: drone, hangar or controlunit. ts integer Sender's uptime in milliseconds. The Pico has no real-time clock, so the backend adds its own reception time for the log. reqId integer Only in requests, responses and commands: identifies the exchange (see Request/response). data object Type-specific content. Omitted when empty.

Units are fixed: metres, metres per second, metres per second squared, degrees, degrees Celsius, percent.

docs.title: State and status
docs.text:
dib/hangar/state 

{ "v": 1, "type": "STATE", "src": "hangar", "ts": 90210,
  "data": { "state": "ALARM", "cause": "DRONE_OFFLINE", "droneDetected": false } }
cause is present only in the ALARM state. The message is published when the state changes and also when droneDetected changes.

dib/drone/state 

{ "v": 1, "type": "STATE", "src": "drone", "ts": 90180,
  "data": { "state": "IN_MISSION" } }

dib/<device>/status 

{ "v": 1, "type": "STATUS", "src": "drone", "ts": 1520,
  "data": { "online": true } }

dib/hangar/door 

{ "v": 1, "type": "DOOR", "src": "hangar", "ts": 91050,
  "data": { "state": "OPENING", "position": 45 } }

dib/hangar/environment 

{ "v": 1, "type": "ENVIRONMENT", "src": "hangar", "ts": 92000,
  "data": { "temperature": 18.5, "humidity": 62, "safe": true } }

dib/drone/telemetry 

{ "v": 1, "type": "TELEMETRY", "src": "drone", "ts": 92300,
  "data": { "battery": 74, "charging": false, "speed": 8.2, "acceleration": 0.4,
            "altitude": 30.0, "groundDistance": 30.0, "distanceFromHangar": 112.5,
            "roll": 2.1, "pitch": -1.4, "progress": 46, "segment": 3, "segments": 6,
            "error": null } }

docs.text:
{ "v": 1, "type": "TAKEOFF_REQ", "src": "drone", "ts": 128450, "reqId": 3482 }

{ "v": 1, "type": "LANDING_REQ", "src": "drone", "ts": 412900, "reqId": 3483 }

{ "v": 1, "type": "AUTH_RESPONSE", "src": "drone", "ts": 413050, "reqId": 3483,
  "data": { "hmac": "9f2c…e71a" } }

docs.text:
{ "v": 1, "type": "CHALLENGE", "src": "hangar", "ts": 389120, "reqId": 3483,
  "data": { "nonce": "4be1a09c37d2f5e8b06a1c9d2e7f4a31" } }

{ "v": 1, "type": "GRANTED", "src": "hangar", "ts": 390800, "reqId": 3483 }

  "data": { "reason": "BAD_WEATHER" } }

docs.title: Commands and replies
docs.text:
dib/cmd/drone, dib/cmd/hangar 

{ "v": 1, "type": "CMD", "src": "controlunit", "ts": 1731690000, "reqId": 57,
  "data": { "command": "START_MISSION" } }
Commands: START_MISSION, RECALL (drone); EMERGENCY_CLOSE, RESET_ALARM (hangar).

dib/<device>/cmd-reply 

{ "v": 1, "type": "CMD_REPLY", "src": "drone", "ts": 95400, "reqId": 57,
  "data": { "accepted": false, "reason": "BATTERY_LOW" } }

docs.title: Request/response
docs.text:
MQTT has no request/response interaction, so it is built on top of publish/subscribe: requests travel on dib/drone/request, responses on dib/hangar/response, and the two are matched by the reqId field.

Request identifiers. The drone generates a new reqId for every take-off or landing request, from a counter initialised with a random value at boot, so that identifiers are not reused after a reboot. All the messages of one exchange carry the same reqId: a landing request, its challenge, the authentication response and the final decision.

Matching and duplicates.

  • The drone accepts only responses whose reqId matches its current request, and ignores all the others (old, duplicated or not addressed to it).
  • The hangar processes one request at a time. A request that arrives while another one is in progress, or a duplicate of the current one, is ignored.
  • Since every message is matched by reqId, receiving one twice (possible with QoS 1) has no effect.

Timeouts. Every wait is bounded, so no device waits forever:

Who waits For what Timeout On expiry Drone GRANTED / DENIED after TAKEOFF_REQ 5 s back to AT_REST, reason NO_RESPONSE Drone CHALLENGE after LANDING_REQ 3 s HOLDING, reason NO_RESPONSE Drone GRANTED / DENIED after AUTH_RESPONSE 5 s HOLDING, reason NO_RESPONSE Drone retry delay in HOLDING 10 s sends a new LANDING_REQ Hangar AUTH_RESPONSE after CHALLENGE 3 s DENIED, reason AUTH_TIMEOUT Hangar drone out after GRANTED (take-off) 15 s ALARM, cause DEPARTURE_TIMEOUT Hangar drone landed after GRANTED (landing) 20 s ALARM, cause LANDING_TIMEOUT

The drone's timeouts after a request are longer than the door movement (about 1.5 s), because the hangar sends GRANTED only when the door is fully open. The values are defaults and can be configured.

docs.title: Authentication handshake
docs.text:
Before evaluating a landing request, the hangar checks that the request really comes from the registered drone. Hangar and drone share a secret key; the drone proves it knows the key without ever sending it.

sequenceDiagram
  participant D as Drone
  participant H as Hangar
  D->>H: LANDING_REQ (reqId)
  Note over H: generate random nonce
  H->>D: CHALLENGE (reqId, nonce)
  Note over D: hmac = HMAC-SHA256(key, message)
  D->>H: AUTH_RESPONSE (reqId, hmac)
  Note over H: compute the same HMAC and compare
  H->>D: GRANTED or DENIED (reqId)

Computation.

  • Key: 32 random bytes, stored in a configuration header that is excluded from version control (secrets.h).
  • Nonce: 16 bytes from the hardware random number generator of the RP2350, sent as a lowercase hex string.
  • Message: the UTF-8 string <nonce>|<droneId>|<reqId>, e.g. 4be1a09c37d2f5e8b06a1c9d2e7f4a31|drone|3483.
  • Answer: HMAC-SHA256(key, message), sent as a lowercase hex string (64 characters).

Verification. The hangar computes the same HMAC and compares the two values in constant time, so the comparison time reveals nothing about the expected value. Each nonce allows a single attempt:

  • match → the hangar evaluates the weather and grants or denies the landing;
  • mismatch → DENIED with AUTH_FAILED;
  • no answer within 3 s → DENIED with AUTH_TIMEOUT.

Why it resists replay. The nonce is new and random for every landing request, so a captured AUTH_RESPONSE matches only the challenge it was computed for. Sent again later, it is checked against a different nonce and fails (EC-8). Including droneId and reqId in the message ties the answer to one drone and one exchange.

Limitation. The key is shared and stored in both firmwares, so anyone who can read a device's flash can obtain it. This is acceptable for the prototype. A real system would use per-device keys in secure storage.

docs.title: Denial reasons
docs.text: Every refusal carries a reason field with one of the following codes, so that the dashboard can show it and the tests can check it.

docs.title: Take-off request
docs.text:
Sent by the hangar in a DENIED message.

Code Meaning BAD_WEATHER Humidity, temperature are above the safety threshold. ALARM_ACTIVE The hangar is in the alarm state and accepts no requests until reset. DRONE_NOT_PRESENT The presence sensor does not detect the drone inside the hangar.

docs.title: Landing request
docs.text:
Sent by the hangar in a DENIED message. All the take-off codes also apply, plus:

Code Meaning AUTH_FAILED The answer to the challenge is wrong. AUTH_TIMEOUT The drone did not answer the challenge in time.

docs.title: Timeouts on the drone side
docs.text:
Not sent by anyone: set by the drone when the hangar does not answer, and published in its telemetry.

Code Meaning NO_RESPONSE No answer to a take-off or landing request within the timeout.

docs.title: Operator commands
docs.text:
Sent by the drone or the hangar in a cmd-reply message.

Code Meaning INVALID_STATE The command is not accepted in the current state (e.g. Recall while at rest). BATTERY_LOW Start mission refused: battery below the minimum take-off level. CAUSE_NOT_CLEARED Reset alarm refused: the cause of the alarm is still present.

docs.title: Control
docs.text: This chapter describes the control architecture shared by the hangar-unit and the drone-unit.

docs.title: Task
docs.text:
The firmware of each unit follows a task-based architecture:

  • the behaviour of the unit is decomposed into a set of concurrent tasks;
  • each task is a well-defined and independent unit of work, with its own period;
  • the behaviour of each task is described by a synchronous FSM (see Behaviour).

All tasks extend the abstract class AbstractTask, which stores the period of the task and the time elapsed since its last execution. Each concrete task implements tick(), which performs one step of its FSM.

The tasks run on a single core, so their concurrency is logical: they do not run in parallel, but their executions are interleaved by the scheduler.

docs.title: Scheduler
docs.text:
Tasks are executed by a cooperative scheduler with a round-robin policy:

  • the scheduler has a base period p, equal to the greatest common divisor of the periods of the tasks (50 ms);
  • the period of every task is a multiple of p;
  • at every period p, the scheduler updates the elapsed time of each task and calls tick() only on the tasks whose period has expired, always in the same order;
  • a timer provides the periodic behaviour: the scheduler waits for the next tick of the timer before starting a new round.

For example, with p = 50 ms the door task (50 ms) runs at every round, the controller (100 ms) every second round, and the environment monitor (2 s) every 40 rounds.

classDiagram
  class AbstractTask {
    <<abstract>>
    -int period
    -int timeElapsed
    +init(int period)
    +updateAndCheckTime(int basePeriod) bool
    +tick()*
  }
  class Scheduler {
    -int basePeriod
    -AbstractTask* tasks[MAX_TASKS]
    -int nTasks
    +init(int basePeriod)
    +addTask(AbstractTask* task) bool
    +schedule()
  }
  class Timer {
    +setupPeriod(int period)
    +waitForNextTick()
  }
  Scheduler o-- "0..*" AbstractTask
  Scheduler --> Timer
  AbstractTask <|-- DoorTask
  AbstractTask <|-- ControllerTask
  AbstractTask <|-- CommTask

docs.title: State pattern
docs.text:
The discrete components of each unit are modelled as FSMs (see Behaviour). The continuous models (flight kinematics, battery) and the hardware drivers are not FSMs.

The larger machines are implemented with the State pattern: each state is a class, and the task that runs the machine holds a reference to the current state. Since the machines are Moore machines, each state class defines three operations:

  • next(): evaluates the guards on the inputs and returns the next state (or itself);
  • onEnter(): emits the messages of the state, once, when the state is entered;
  • outputs(): applies the level outputs of the state (door command, LEDs, flight dynamics).
classDiagram
  class AbstractTask {
    <<abstract>>
    +tick()*
  }
  class Context {
    -State* current
    +tick()
  }
  class State {
    <<interface>>
    +onEnter(Context ctx)
    +outputs(Context ctx)
    +next(Context ctx) State*
  }
  class ConcreteStateA {
    +onEnter(Context ctx)
    +outputs(Context ctx)
    +next(Context ctx) State*
  }
  class ConcreteStateB {
    +onEnter(Context ctx)
    +outputs(Context ctx)
    +next(Context ctx) State*
  }
  AbstractTask <|-- Context
  Context o-- State : current
  State <|.. ConcreteStateA
  State <|.. ConcreteStateB

The context is the task itself: each call to tick() performs one reaction of the machine.

void Context::tick() {
  State* nextState = current->next(*this);
  if (nextState != current) {
    current = nextState;
    current->onEnter(*this);
  }
  current->outputs(*this);
}

Timers and counters (timeouts, retry delays) are variables of the context, incremented at every reaction, as in an extended FSM.

All state objects are created once, at start-up; no memory is allocated while the system is running. Small machines with two or three states (button, presence monitor) are implemented with a plain enum and a switch, which is simpler and equivalent.

docs.title: Communication between tasks
docs.text:
Tasks never call each other: they communicate through a shared object, BlackBoard, passed by reference to each task when it is created. A task reads its inputs from BlackBoard and writes its outputs into it.

Shared data are of two kinds:

  • levels describe the current situation (e.g. whether the environment is safe, the position of the door). They are overwritten at every update, and readers always use the latest value;
  • events describe something that happened once (e.g. a button press, a request received). The producer sets a flag, and the consumer clears it after handling the event, so that each event is handled exactly once. Where events can arrive faster than the consumer's period, a queue replaces the flag.

The only code that runs outside the scheduler is the MQTT callback. It never writes BlackBoard directly: it pushes the received message into a queue, which the communication task empties at its next execution.

flowchart LR
  MQTT((MQTT callback)) -->|push| Q[[Message queue]]
  Q -->|pop| C[Comm task]
  C --> SD[(BlackBoard)]
  S[Sensor tasks] --> SD
  SD --> F[FSM tasks]
  F --> SD
  SD --> A[Actuator tasks]

A value written by a task becomes visible to the tasks that run after it in the same round, or in the next round. Since all machines are Moore machines, their outputs do not depend on the inputs of the same reaction, so the order in which the scheduler runs the tasks does not affect the correctness of the system.

docs.title: MQTT integration
docs.text: Each unit has a communication task (CommTask), the only part of the firmware that talks to the network. It connects to Wi-Fi and to the broker, receives and sends messages, and keeps the rest of the system independent from MQTT. The common behaviour is implemented in an abstract CommTask; each unit extends it with its own topics and message handling.

docs.title: Receiving messages
docs.text:
The MQTT library delivers incoming messages through a callback, which runs outside the scheduler. To keep the tasks synchronous, the callback does only one thing: it copies the message into the inbox, a fixed-size queue, and returns.

At each execution, CommTask empties the inbox and passes every message to the dispatcher, which:

  1. parses the JSON envelope and discards malformed messages or messages with an unknown protocol version;
  2. discards messages not accepted in the current state of the unit (e.g. a request while another one is in progress, a response with an unknown reqId) or answers them directly (e.g. INVALID_STATE for an operator command);
  3. turns every accepted message into a blackboard update: a level (e.g. the drone's state) or an event (e.g. a take-off request).

The acceptance rules depend on the unit and are described in Hangar and Drone.

If the inbox is full, the new message is dropped and a counter is incremented. With QoS 1 and the request timeouts of the protocol, a dropped message is recovered by a retry.

docs.title: Sending messages
docs.text:
Tasks never publish directly. The messages emitted on entry into a state are placed in the outbox, a fixed-size queue in the blackboard, and CommTask publishes them at its next execution. CommTask also publishes:

  • the state of the unit (retained) whenever it changes;
  • periodic data (telemetry, environment) at the period set for each unit;
  • the online status right after every connection.

docs.title: Connection management
docs.text:
Connecting to Wi-Fi and to the broker can take seconds, which would block every other task. The connection is therefore managed by a small FSM inside CommTask, which makes at most one connection attempt per execution:

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> DISCONNECTED

  state "DISCONNECTED" as DISCONNECTED
  DISCONNECTED : connected = false
  state "WIFI_CONNECTING" as WIFI_CONNECTING
  WIFI_CONNECTING : connected = false
  state "MQTT_CONNECTING" as MQTT_CONNECTING
  MQTT_CONNECTING : connected = false
  state "CONNECTED" as CONNECTED
  CONNECTED : connected = true
  CONNECTED : on entry subscribe and publish online and state

  DISCONNECTED --> WIFI_CONNECTING : backoff expired
  WIFI_CONNECTING --> MQTT_CONNECTING : wifi up
  WIFI_CONNECTING --> DISCONNECTED : attempt failed
  MQTT_CONNECTING --> CONNECTED : broker accepted
  MQTT_CONNECTING --> DISCONNECTED : attempt failed
  CONNECTED --> DISCONNECTED : wifi or broker lost
  • After a failed attempt, the delay before the next one doubles, up to a maximum (e.g. 1 s, 2 s, 4 s … 30 s), so that a missing network does not waste the processor.
  • When connecting, the client registers its Last Will (offline on dib/<unit>/status).
  • On entering CONNECTED, it subscribes to its topics, publishes online and republishes its current state, so that the other components are up to date.
  • While disconnected, the unit keeps working autonomously: the FSMs continue to run, and messages placed in the outbox are discarded. The protocol does not depend on them being delivered later, thanks to the timeouts and the retained state.

The connected flag is written in the blackboard, so other tasks can show it (e.g. on the display).

docs.title: Hangar
docs.text: This chapter describes how the control architecture of Control is applied to the hangar unit. The behaviour of each state machine is defined in Behaviour; here we describe how the parts are organised and how they exchange data.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
The hangar firmware is a set of periodic tasks that never call each other: they communicate only through a shared HangarBlackboard. Input tasks read the sensors and write their values into the blackboard; the controller takes decisions on those values; output tasks drive the actuators; HangarComm connects the blackboard to the MQTT broker.

flowchart LR
  subgraph Sensors
    IR[IR sensor]
    DHT[DHT11]
    PB[Reset button]
  end

  subgraph Inputs [Input tasks]
    PRES[PresenceTask]
    ENV[EnvMonitorTask]
    BTN[ButtonTask]
  end

  BB[(HangarBlackboard)]
  CTRL[ControllerTask]
  COMM[HangarComm]
  BR[(MQTT broker)]

  subgraph Outputs [Output tasks]
    DOOR[DoorTask]
    STAT[StatusTask]
  end

  subgraph Actuators
    SERVO[Servo]
    TL[Traffic light]
    LCD[Display]
  end

  IR --> PRES
  DHT --> ENV
  PB --> BTN
  PRES --> BB
  ENV --> BB
  BTN --> BB
  BB <--> CTRL
  BB <--> COMM
  COMM <--> BR
  BB <--> DOOR
  BB --> STAT
  DOOR --> SERVO
  STAT --> TL

Only ControllerTask takes decisions. The other tasks either translate a physical signal into a value (input tasks), or a value into a physical action (output tasks), or messages into values and back (HangarComm).

docs.title: 2. Tasks
docs.text:
Task Period Behaviour Reads Writes HangarComm 50 ms Connection FSM, dispatcher (Control) hangarState, doorState, doorPosition, environment, droneDetected, outbox droneState, droneOnline, connected, request events PresenceTask 100 ms Presence monitor FSM (4.4) IR sensor droneDetected EnvMonitorTask 2 s Environment monitor FSM (4.3) DHT11 envOk, temperature, humidity ButtonTask 50 ms Button FSM (4.5) reset button resetFromButton ControllerTask 100 ms Controller FSM (4.1) inputs and events above, doorState doorCmd, hangarState, reason, cause, outbox DoorTask 50 ms Door FSM (4.2) doorCmd doorState, doorPosition, servo StatusTask 250 ms Status indicator (4.6) hangarState, reason, cause, environment traffic light, display

The section numbers in the Behaviour column refer to Behaviour.

Order of execution. The tasks are registered in the scheduler in the order of the table: communication and inputs first, then the controller, then the outputs. In this way, within the same round:

  • the controller decides on the freshest inputs, including the messages just received;
  • the actuators apply the commands the controller has just produced.

A command therefore reaches the door in the same round in which it was decided. The only one-round delay concerns outgoing messages: the controller places them in the outbox after HangarComm has run, so they are published at the next round, at most 50 ms later.

Base period. The scheduler runs with a base period of 50 ms, the greatest common divisor of the task periods. The timer keeps a fixed grid of ticks: if a round overruns, the missed ticks are skipped and counted, without shifting the following ones.

docs.title: 3. Blackboard
docs.text: HangarBlackboard holds all the data shared by the tasks. It is created once at start-up and passed by reference to every task. Every field has exactly one writer.

docs.title: Levels
docs.text:
Levels describe the current situation and are overwritten at every update.

Field Writer Readers droneDetected PresenceTask ControllerTask, HangarComm envOk, temperature, humidity EnvMonitorTask ControllerTask, StatusTask, HangarComm doorState, doorPosition DoorTask ControllerTask, StatusTask, HangarComm doorCmd ControllerTask DoorTask hangarState, reason, cause ControllerTask StatusTask, HangarComm droneState, droneOnline HangarComm ControllerTask connected HangarComm StatusTask

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Events describe something that happened once. They are posted by one task and consumed exactly once by another.

Event Posted by Consumed by request (type, reqId) HangarComm ControllerTask authResponse (reqId, HMAC) HangarComm ControllerTask emergencyClose HangarComm ControllerTask resetFromDashboard HangarComm ControllerTask resetFromButton ButtonTask ControllerTask

The reset has two sources, the dashboard and the local button, so it is modelled as two separate events: a single shared flag would have two writers. The controller handles them in the same way.

docs.title: Outbox
docs.text:
The outbox is a fixed-size queue of outgoing messages (CHALLENGE, GRANTED, DENIED). ControllerTask adds a message when it enters a state that emits one; HangarComm empties the queue and publishes the messages. In this way only HangarComm depends on MQTT.

The state of the hangar, the door and the environment are not placed in the outbox: HangarComm reads them directly from the levels and publishes them when they change.

docs.title: 4.2 Controller
docs.text:
The controller FSM is implemented with the State pattern. ControllerTask is the context: it holds the current state and the variables of the extended FSM (current request, timer, pending emergency closure). Each of the nine states of the controller FSM is a class implementing State. The states are stateless objects, created once at start-up: everything that must be remembered between reactions lives in ControllerTask.

This separation has two benefits:

  • testability: since tasks depend only on interfaces, they compile in the native environment and are tested on the PC with fake devices (e.g. a fake servo that records the angles it receives);
  • replaceability: changing a device (e.g. a different display) requires a new driver, not a change in the tasks.
